subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which three colours are the primary colours in traditional painting colour theory?
questions.explain: The primary colours red, yellow and blue cannot be mixed from other pigments and form the basis of the colour wheel.

questions.q: Which set lists the three secondary colours?
questions.explain: Secondary colours (orange, green and violet) are each made by mixing two primary colours together.

questions.q: On the colour wheel, which colour is complementary to red?
questions.explain: Complementary colours sit opposite one another on the colour wheel, so red pairs with green.

questions.q: In colour theory, what is a 'tint'?
options: A colour mixed with its complementary
questions.explain: Adding white to a hue lightens it to produce a tint.

questions.q: An artist adds black to a pure hue to darken it. What is this darker version called?
questions.explain: Adding black to a colour produces a shade, a darker version of the original hue.

questions.q: Which group is usually described as the 'warm' colours?
questions.explain: Reds, oranges and yellows are classed as warm colours, while blues, greens and violets are cool.

questions.q: What best describes a harmonious (analogous) colour scheme?
options: Colours that sit next to each other on the colour wheel
Colours directly opposite on the colour wheel
A single hue with added white
questions.explain: Harmonious or analogous colours are neighbours on the wheel, giving a unified, restful effect.

questions.q: Which statement best describes watercolour paint?
options: A water-based paint that is usually transparent
An oil-based paint that dries very slowly
A thick, always-opaque paint used straight from the tube
A paint made by mixing pigment with egg
questions.explain: Watercolour is a water-based, generally transparent medium applied in thin layers, often on paper.

questions.q: Traditional oil paint is made by binding pigment with which of the following?
options: A drying oil such as linseed oil
questions.explain: Oil paint mixes pigment with a drying oil, commonly linseed oil, giving it a slow drying time.

questions.q: How does gouache differ from ordinary watercolour?
options: It is opaque rather than transparent
It is oil-based rather than water-based
It can only be used on canvas
questions.explain: Gouache is a water-based paint like watercolour but contains more pigment and filler, making it opaque.

questions.q: A student wants a water-based paint that dries quickly so they can build up several layers within one lesson. Which paint best suits this?
questions.explain: Acrylic is water-based and dries rapidly, allowing layers to be added quickly.

questions.q: Which term describes paint applied thickly so that it stands up from the surface and holds brush or knife marks?
questions.explain: Impasto is a thick, textured application of paint that leaves visible ridges on the surface.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of applying a glaze in painting?
options: To lay a thin, transparent layer of colour over a dry layer beneath
To scratch lines into wet paint
To apply paint in thick opaque lumps
To dab on separate dots of colour
questions.explain: Glazing uses thin, transparent layers to modify the colour and depth of the layers below.

questions.q: In watercolour painting, what is a 'wash'?
options: A thin, diluted layer of colour spread evenly over an area
A thick raised line of paint
A patch of paint scraped away with a blade
A dry, textured drag of stiff paint
questions.explain: A wash is watercolour heavily diluted with water and brushed on as a broad, even, transparent layer.

questions.q: An artist wants a rough, three-dimensional surface where each brushstroke can be clearly felt and seen. Which technique should they use?
questions.explain: Impasto builds thick, raised paint so individual strokes create a tactile, textured surface.

questions.q: A student wants colours to blend into one another with soft, blurred edges, such as a sky at sunset. Which approach is most suitable?
options: Applying stiff paint with a palette knife
questions.explain: Applying wet paint into a still-wet layer lets colours run together for soft, blended edges.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the formal elements of art?
questions.explain: The formal elements include line, shape, form, tone, colour, texture and pattern; glazing, gouache and impasto are media or techniques.

questions.q: What does the formal element 'tone' refer to?
options: The lightness or darkness of an area
The rough or smooth feel of a surface
questions.explain: Tone describes how light or dark something is and is used to suggest form and depth.

questions.q: In the formal elements, how does 'form' differ from 'shape'?
options: Form is three-dimensional, while shape is flat and two-dimensional
Form is always coloured, while shape is always black
Form refers only to texture, while shape refers to line
There is no difference between them
questions.explain: Shape is a flat, two-dimensional area, whereas form describes a three-dimensional object or the illusion of one.

questions.q: A student uses close cross-hatched brushstrokes to make one side of a painted object appear darker and rounded. Which formal element are they mainly working with?
questions.explain: Building up dark and light areas to suggest a rounded, shaded surface is working with tone.
